lead: Gears pass rotation and torque from one shaft to another at a fixed speed ratio, with no slip. The law of gearing says what tooth shape makes the ratio truly constant: at every instant the common normal at the contact point must pass through one fixed point, the pitch point. The involute profile meets this law and also forgives a small error in centre distance, so almost every power gear uses it. Gears sit in every two-wheeler gearbox and in the pump set on a Chennai terrace.
prereq: You need: school geometry of circles and tangents, and the pitch-line speed v = πdn/60 used for belt drives.

blocks.text: Gears are grouped by how their shafts sit. Spur gears have straight teeth and join parallel shafts; they are simple and efficient but noisy at high speed, because a whole tooth width engages at once. Helical gears also join parallel shafts, with teeth at a helix angle: they run quieter and carry more load, but push the shaft axially. Bevel gears are cut on cones and join intersecting shafts, usually at 90°. A worm and worm wheel join crossed shafts and give a large reduction in one step. A rack is a gear of infinite radius that turns rotation into straight-line motion, as in a car steering rack. An internal gear has its teeth inside a ring; the pinion runs inside it and both turn the same way.

Every calculation starts at the pitch circle: the imaginary circle on which the two gears roll without slipping. Let d be the pitch circle diameter in mm and z the number of teeth. The module is m = d/z, in mm; a 4 mm module means 4 mm of pitch diameter for every tooth, and modules come from a standard series (1, 1.25, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10 mm). The circular pitch is the distance from a point on one tooth to the same point on the next, measured along the pitch circle: p = πd/z = πm. In inch units the diametral pitch is P = z/d with d in inches (teeth per inch of diameter), so m = 25.4/P.

Tooth heights follow the module. For standard 20° full-depth teeth the addendum (pitch circle to tip) is ha = m and the dedendum (pitch circle to root) is hf = 1.25m. The addendum circle passes through the tips, da = d + 2m; the dedendum circle passes through the roots, df = d − 2.5m. Clearance is c = 0.25m, working depth 2m and whole depth 2.25m. On the pitch circle the tooth thickness and the space width are each p/2 in theory; the space is made slightly wider, and the gap between the non-driving flanks of a meshing pair is the backlash. Face width b is the tooth length along the shaft.

The line of action is the common tangent to the two base circles; tooth contact always lies on it. The pressure angle φ is the angle between this line and the common tangent to the two pitch circles at the pitch point; 20° is standard, 14½° is old practice. The base circle, db = d cos φ, is the circle the involute grows from. For two external gears the centre distance is a = m(z1 + z2)/2; for an internal pair a = m(z2 − z1)/2, with z2 the internal gear.

sections.h3: The law of gearing, the involute and contact ratio

blocks.text: At any instant two teeth touch at one point. Draw the common normal to the two profiles there. If this normal cuts the line of centres O1O2 at a fixed point P, similar triangles give ω1/ω2 = O2P/O1P, a constant. That is the law of gearing. If the normal wanders, the ratio changes tooth by tooth and the drive vibrates.

An involute is the curve traced by the end of a taut string unwound from a base circle. Its normal at every point is tangent to the base circle. For two involute teeth the common normal is therefore the common tangent to both base circles, a line fixed in space, so it always cuts O1O2 at the same point P and ω1/ω2 = d2/d1 = z2/z1. If the centre distance grows a little, the base circles do not change, so the ratio does not change either; only the working pressure angle and the backlash grow.

Contact begins where the gear's addendum circle cuts the line of action and ends where the pinion's addendum circle cuts it. That length is the path of contact; divided by the base pitch pb = πm cos φ it gives the contact ratio, the average number of tooth pairs in mesh. It must be more than 1, and 1.4 to 1.8 is usual for spur gears. Interference happens when a gear tip would touch the pinion below its base circle, where there is no involute. During cutting the cutter then removes metal from the pinion root; this undercutting is the damage interference does, and it weakens the tooth. A 20° full-depth pinion needs about 17 or more teeth to escape it, or a profile shift. Tooth strength itself is the subject of spur gear design.

examples.question: A 20° full-depth involute spur pair has z<sub>1</sub> = 20, z<sub>2</sub> = 60 and module 4 mm. Find both pitch diameters, the centre distance, both base circle diameters and the velocity ratio.
steps: Pitch diameters: d<sub>1</sub> = m z<sub>1</sub> = 4 × 20 = 80 mm and d<sub>2</sub> = m z<sub>2</sub> = 4 × 60 = 240 mm.
Centre distance (external pair): a = (d<sub>1</sub> + d<sub>2</sub>)/2 = (80 + 240)/2 = 160 mm.
Base circles: d<sub>b</sub> = d cos φ, with cos 20° = 0.93969. d<sub>b1</sub> = 80 × 0.93969 = 75.18 mm and d<sub>b2</sub> = 240 × 0.93969 = 225.53 mm.
Velocity ratio: ω<sub>1</sub>/ω<sub>2</sub> = z<sub>2</sub>/z<sub>1</sub> = 60/20 = 3. The pinion turns three times for one turn of the gear.
examples.answer: d<sub>1</sub> = 80 mm, d<sub>2</sub> = 240 mm, a = 160 mm, d<sub>b1</sub> = 75.18 mm, d<sub>b2</sub> = 225.53 mm, velocity ratio 3.

examples.question: For the same pair (addendum = m = 4 mm) find the path of approach, the path of recess, the path of contact and the contact ratio.
steps: Radii: r<sub>1</sub> = 40 mm, r<sub>2</sub> = 120 mm; addendum radii r<sub>a1</sub> = 44 mm, r<sub>a2</sub> = 124 mm; base radii r<sub>b1</sub> = 37.588 mm, r<sub>b2</sub> = 112.763 mm.
Path of approach (set by the gear tip): √(r<sub>a2</sub>² − r<sub>b2</sub>²) − r<sub>2</sub> sin φ = √(124² − 112.763²) − 120 × 0.34202 = 51.580 − 41.042 = 10.537 mm.
Path of recess (set by the pinion tip): √(r<sub>a1</sub>² − r<sub>b1</sub>²) − r<sub>1</sub> sin φ = √(44² − 37.588²) − 40 × 0.34202 = 22.873 − 13.681 = 9.192 mm.
Base pitch p<sub>b</sub> = πm cos φ = π × 4 × 0.93969 = 11.809 mm.
examples.answer: Approach 10.54 mm, recess 9.19 mm, path of contact 19.73 mm, contact ratio 1.67: two pairs of teeth share the load for about two thirds of the time.

traps: Module uses the pitch circle: m = d/z. Using the tip (addendum) diameter or the base diameter gives a wrong module.
Contact ratio is the path of contact over the base pitch πm cos φ, or the arc of contact over p = πm; a path over p is wrong.
The law of gearing is about the common normal at the contact point, not the common tangent. Examiners test this wording.
Diametral pitch is in inch units: P = z/d with d in inches, and m = 25.4/P. Mixing mm with P gives nonsense.
Undercutting is not a cure; it is the damage interference causes when a pinion has too few teeth. The cures are more teeth, a profile shift or a stub tooth.

quiz.q: Define module and give its unit.
quiz.a: m = d/z, where d is the pitch circle diameter and z the number of teeth. Unit: mm.

quiz.q: Why does an involute profile satisfy the law of gearing?
quiz.a: The normal to an involute is tangent to its base circle. For two involutes the common normal is the common tangent to both base circles, a fixed line, so it always cuts the line of centres at the same pitch point and the ratio stays constant.

quiz.q: A 20° pair has z<sub>1</sub> = 18, z<sub>2</sub> = 54 and module 3 mm. Find d<sub>1</sub>, d<sub>2</sub>, the centre distance and the pinion base circle diameter.
Find the circular pitch and the addendum circle diameter of a 30-tooth gear of module 5 mm.
The centre distance of an involute pair is increased by 0.5 mm. What happens to the velocity ratio, the pressure angle and the backlash?
quiz.a: The ratio stays z<sub>2</sub>/z<sub>1</sub> because the base circles do not change. The working pressure angle increases slightly, the backlash increases and the contact ratio falls a little, but the teeth still mesh correctly.

quiz.q: Why does undercutting appear on a small pinion meshing with a large gear?
quiz.a: The large gear's tip would reach the pinion flank below the pinion's base circle, where there is no involute. During generation the cutter removes that metal from the pinion root, which thins and weakens the tooth. More teeth (about 17 or more for 20° full depth) or a profile shift avoid it.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern gearboxes use profile-modified and tip-relieved teeth to cut noise, and some use asymmetric teeth whose driving flank has a larger pressure angle. Search next: profile shift, tip relief, transmission error, gear metrology.
